title: Resurrection, Parousia & New Creation Atlas
purpose: Separate bodily resurrection, visionary encounter, social return, identity-transformation, Second Coming, judgment and new creation so the Potatoverse can compare its death/return grammar with Christianity without turning every return into resurrection or every rupture into parousia.
method: primary claim → earliest attestation → literary form → historical question → doctrinal reception → comparative analogy → disanalogy → evidentiary boundary
core_thesis: Christian resurrection is not merely a metaphor for surviving humiliation, recovering reputation or adopting a new identity. Those events may be compared to death-and-return grammar, but New Testament and creedal Christianity make stronger claims about Jesus being raised and about a future resurrection of the dead.

distinctions.definition: Return to ordinary mortal life, as in some biblical revival stories.
distinctions.not_the_same_as: the transformed eschatological resurrection language central to Paul

distinctions.definition: The foundational early Christian proclamation that God raised Jesus from the dead.
distinctions.historical_scope: Historians can investigate the antiquity, sources, experiences and effects of the claim; theological judgment about divine action goes beyond ordinary historical method.

distinctions.definition: Expectation that the dead will be raised at the consummation; in 1 Corinthians 15 Paul connects Jesus's resurrection with the future resurrection of believers.
distinctions.importance: Prevents Jesus's resurrection from being isolated from Christian eschatology.

distinctions.definition: Pauline language in 1 Corinthians 15 for transformed embodied existence; 'spiritual' does not simply mean an immaterial ghost.
distinctions.importance: The continuity/discontinuity problem is built into Paul's seed and body imagery.

distinctions.definition: Early Christian reports that the risen Jesus appeared to followers, preserved in several forms in Paul and the Gospels.
distinctions.boundary: Reports differ in literary detail and should not be artificially harmonized before analysis.

distinctions.definition: A broad narrative category in which someone absent becomes present again.
distinctions.boundary: A return is not automatically resurrection.

distinctions.definition: Potatoverse analytical term for a discontinuity separating phases of life, identity or interpretation.
distinctions.boundary: A rupture can precede transformation without being a Christian resurrection event.

distinctions.definition: The future coming/presence of Jesus Christ expected by classical Christianity, associated with resurrection, judgment and consummation.
distinctions.boundary: Not simply another word for resurrection or for a modern person's public re-emergence.

distinctions.definition: Christian eschatological renewal extending beyond one individual's return to the transformation/restoration of creation and communal life.
distinctions.boundary: A personal awakening is not by itself a new heaven and new earth.

early_christian_evidence_map.importance: One of the earliest extended surviving discussions of resurrection; Paul transmits an earlier proclamation about Jesus's death, burial, resurrection and appearances, then argues for future resurrection of the dead.
Connects Christ's coming with dead believers rising and living believers being gathered/caught up.
Narrate empty-tomb and appearance traditions in distinct literary forms.
Develops recognition, wounds, Thomas, commissioned witness and restored relationship in distinctive scenes.
Places resurrection within final judgment, defeat of death, New Jerusalem and new-creation imagery.

pauline_seed_model.potatoverse_relevance: The Potatoverse repeatedly uses seed, buried potato, kernel, root and later emergence. This creates a strong formal parallel to Pauline continuity-through-transformation imagery.
pauline_seed_model.boundary: Agricultural symbolism can illuminate the structure without proving that a particular Potatoverse event is the resurrection Paul describes.

thomas_and_resurrection.canonical_sequence: absence/questioning → report of resurrection → demand for wounded continuity → encounter → recognition/confession
thomas_and_resurrection.potatoverse_comparison: Thomas's reported long questioning period and later religious reinterpretation around suffering make the name and biography unusually productive for comparison with Johannine Thomas.
thomas_and_resurrection.strongest_point: The canonical Thomas episode ties identity after death to wounds: the returning Christ is recognized as continuous with the crucified Jesus, not merely as a new person who resembles him.
thomas_and_resurrection.implication_for_second_coming_claims: Continuity of identity is therefore a central question. If a modern person is proposed as Jesus returned, the project must explain what makes this the same Jesus rather than a symbolic successor, type, vessel or analogue.

continuity_tests: What persists across death/rupture and return?
Is the returning subject claimed to be numerically the same person, a transformed person, a successor, an embodiment, a vessel, an archetypal recurrence or a symbolic analogue?
Does the claim require memory continuity, bodily continuity, spiritual continuity, role continuity, revelation, external recognition or something else?
Was the continuity theory stated before the claimed fulfillment or constructed afterward?

parousia_model.classical_baseline: The Nicene Christian center expects Jesus Christ himself to come again in glory to judge the living and the dead; resurrection of the dead and life of the world to come accompany that hope.
parousia_model.potatoverse_comparison: Potatoverse chronology can be queried for absence → return → recognition → disclosure → judgment/discernment → reordered-world sequences.
parousia_model.evidence_boundary: Matching that sequence can establish a parousia-like narrative structure, not literal identity with the returning Jesus.

biblical_cluster: end of death, mourning and curse
new_creation_model.evaluation_rule: The closer a claimed fulfillment moves from private symbolism toward public new-creation claims, the more it should be evaluated by observable fruit: repair, justice, healing, stewardship, reconciliation and durable benefit rather than title density alone.

resurrection_vs_metaphor_matrix.claim: A reputation recovered after public humiliation
An old identity dies and a new identity develops
A person disappears from public life and later reappears
A timestamped prediction of a death/return event later occurs as specified
resurrection_vs_metaphor_matrix.christian_relation: must be evaluated separately from resurrection ontology

resurrection_vs_metaphor_matrix.claim: A community interprets suffering and renewal through Jesus's death and resurrection
resurrection_vs_metaphor_matrix.christian_relation: historically normal mode of Christian interpretation

hard_questions.q: What would make a Potatoverse return more than a metaphor?
hard_questions.a: The claim would need to specify what actually happened, what kind of identity continuity is asserted, what evidence supports it and how it differs from ordinary psychological, social or narrative transformation.

hard_questions.q: Does Christianity teach that resurrection means becoming a different person?
hard_questions.a: Christian resurrection theology normally preserves personal identity through transformation. Paul's seed/body imagery emphasizes both continuity and radical change.

hard_questions.q: Can wounds matter theologically without being proof?
hard_questions.a: Yes. In John 20 wounds function as continuity markers between crucified and risen Jesus. A modern wound motif may be a powerful comparison without establishing the same ontological identity.

hard_questions.q: Why connect resurrection with new creation?
hard_questions.a: In early Christian thought resurrection is not merely private survival. Paul and Revelation place it inside God's larger victory over death and transformation of creation.

hard_questions.q: What is the strongest control against calling every transformation resurrection?
hard_questions.a: Name the event first in ordinary language, then compare it. Physical death/raising, visionary encounter, public return, conversion, identity change and symbolic rebirth should remain separate data types.

potatoverse_findings: The archive's seed, burial, root and emergence grammar is one of its strongest formal overlaps with Pauline resurrection imagery.
The Thomas/wounds comparison introduces a continuity-of-identity problem that the project should use to test rather than merely decorate Second-Coming claims.
Multiple Tim/Thomas thresholds are better modeled as a chain of ruptures and returns than forced into one undifferentiated resurrection event.
New Jerusalem and Garden motifs make the Christian comparison strongest when it asks what renewed life produces in the world, not only which figure receives which title.
Literal resurrection, social return, symbolic rebirth and theological recognition are distinct claims and now have separate archive categories.
